title: Risk of an individual stock vs a portfolio
subtitle: Risk management
openingQuestion: You have VND 200 million. Which option below has LOWER overall risk, assuming similar long-term expected return?
openingOptions: Dump it all into the stock of the company you work for because you understand that company best
Dump the entire VND 200 million into a single stock that many people praise as 'promising'
Split the VND 200 million across 15-20 stocks in many different sectors, or an ETF tracking a broad index like VN30
All options carry the same risk, since the amount put in is VND 200 million in each case
explanation: Diversification (spreading capital across many stocks/sectors) helps reduce unsystematic risk - the risk specific to each individual business - without necessarily sacrificing long-term expected return, because the stocks in the portfolio don't move entirely in the same direction as each other.

diagram.label: An individual stock: risk specific to that business

realWorldExample.description: Many investors put most of their portfolio into real-estate stocks during 2021 when the sector was running hot. When Vietnam's corporate-bond market hit a confidence crisis in late 2022, a wave of real-estate stocks fell 60-80% from their peak. Investors who diversified into consumer goods, technology (like FPT), and banking (like VCB) suffered far less damage than those concentrated in a single sector.

quiz.question: What is unsystematic risk (diversifiable risk)?
options: A type of risk found only in bonds, not in stocks
Risk affecting the whole market, like inflation or interest rates
A type of risk that cannot be reduced by any measure at all
Risk specific to one company or sector
quiz.explanation: Unsystematic risk is tied to each individual business/sector. When you diversify your portfolio across many businesses/sectors that aren't fully correlated, a bad event at one company won't drag down the entire portfolio.

quiz.question: How does systematic risk differ from unsystematic risk?
options: It affects the whole market and can't be eliminated through diversification
It only affects one specific company, not the broader market
It can be eliminated entirely if you buy enough different stocks no matter which sector or cycle is involved
It's a concept that doesn't exist in the Vietnamese market
quiz.explanation: Systematic risk affects nearly the entire market at once (like the Covid-19 pandemic or a global financial crisis), so diversifying a stock portfolio doesn't eliminate this type of risk - you need other tools like diversifying across asset classes (stocks, bonds, cash) to reduce it.

quiz.question: Why is a VN30-tracking ETF usually considered lower risk than an individual stock within that basket?
options: Because an ETF always earns a higher return than any individual stock precisely the mechanism diversification relies on
Because a basket of 30 stocks means one bad ticker only affects a portion
Because an ETF's price is unaffected by market volatility
Because every ETF is guaranteed by the State so it can't lose money
quiz.explanation: A VN30-tracking ETF allocates capital across 30 different stocks at a set weighting. If one stock in the basket falls sharply for its own reasons, the impact on the fund's total value is diluted by the other 29 stocks - this is exactly the mechanism through which diversification reduces unsystematic risk.

quiz.question: An investor buys 10 stocks but all 10 are banks. What's the problem with this level of diversification?
options: All ten tickers share the same sector risk group so they can hardly offset each other
No problem at all - ten tickers already eliminate unsystematic risk
The only issue is the trading cost and effort of tracking ten tickers increases
This portfolio is only risky if the weighting across the tickers isn't split evenly
quiz.explanation: Diversification works because assets don't move in the same rhythm. Ten bank stocks react almost identically to interest rates, bad debt, and credit policy, so you're still essentially placing one single bet - just split into ten pieces.

quiz.question: Adding more stocks to a portfolio reduces unsystematic risk, but how does that benefit change as the number of tickers increases?
options: It only starts working once the portfolio exceeds thirty tickers across different sectors
It increases: the more tickers, the more each additional one reduces risk
It stays constant: each added stock reduces risk by exactly the same amount as the one before which is exactly why concentration still counts as risk
It diminishes: the first few tickers contribute almost all the benefit, later ones add very little
quiz.explanation: The benefit of diversification diminishes very quickly: most of the specific risk disappears within about twenty to thirty tickers across different sectors, after which adding more mostly just increases monitoring effort. The remaining risk is market risk, and can't be eliminated by buying more.

keyTakeaways: Unsystematic risk (risk specific to each business/sector) can be significantly reduced by diversifying a portfolio across many different stocks and sectors
Systematic risk (risk to the whole market, like a recession or inflation) can't be fully eliminated just by diversifying stocks - it requires a more diverse asset allocation
A single stock, no matter how 'good', still carries much higher concentration risk than a diversified portfolio or a broad-index ETF
Diversification doesn't mean buying a huge random number of tickers, but choosing stocks/sectors with low correlation to each other to effectively reduce overall risk

practicePrompt.question: You have VND 300 million. A friend advises putting it all into the stock of the company where you work because you 'understand that company best'. Based on the concept of unsystematic risk, is this advice reasonable?
options: Not reasonable - understanding a company well still leaves all-in capital exposed to concentration risk
Reasonable, because understanding the company absolutely thoroughly would eliminate all possible risk when investing in that stock
Reasonable, because employees within a company always have a superior information advantage over every outside investor
Unrelated to the concept of unsystematic risk at all, since this is purely a personal decision
practicePrompt.explanation: Understanding a company well doesn't eliminate concentration risk - dumping all your capital into one business still carries high unsystematic risk, while diversifying across many sectors is what actually reduces that type of risk.

summary.keyIdea: Unsystematic risk (risk specific to each business/sector) can be significantly reduced by diversifying a portfolio across many different stocks and sectors
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Systematic risk (risk to the whole market, like a recession or inflation) can't be fully eliminated just by diversifying stocks - it requires a more diverse asset allocation

application.title: Count your level of concentration
application.message: List out your current investments, calculate the percentage of your largest ticker relative to your total portfolio - if it exceeds 20-30%, consider whether that concentration risk is intentional.
application.secondary: A concrete percentage is far clearer than a vague feeling of 'probably fine'.

sections.text: There's a question that sounds simple but many beginners overlook: if two portfolios have the same expected return, why choose a portfolio with only one stock instead of one with twenty? The answer lies in the concept of concentration risk.
Two types of risk to distinguish

Risk in stock investing splits into two types. Unsystematic risk is risk specific to each business or sector: poor governance, losing a major contract, a new competitor, a specific sector crisis. This type of risk CAN be significantly reduced by diversifying - not dumping all your capital into one business or one sector.

Conversely, systematic risk is risk affecting nearly the entire market at once: an economic recession, high inflation, interest-rate changes, a global financial crisis, a pandemic. This type of risk CANNOT be eliminated just by buying more different stocks, because when the broader market collapses, most stocks fall along with it, even if to varying degrees.
Why an individual stock is riskier than a portfolio

Suppose you put 100% of your capital into a steel company's stock. If the steel sector faces an oversupply crisis and steel prices fall sharply, your entire asset base is directly affected. But if you split your capital across 20 stocks in many sectors (banking, technology, consumer goods, steel, real estate...), the steel-sector shock only affects a small portion of your portfolio, while the other sectors could still be stable or growing, offsetting some of the damage.

items: Unsystematic risk: risk specific to a business/sector - reduced by diversification
Systematic risk: risk to the whole market - not reduced just by diversifying stocks
The more diversified a portfolio (many sectors, low correlation with each other), the more effectively unsystematic risk is diluted
A broad-index ETF (like VN30) is a simple, low-cost way to diversify for beginners

concepts.def: Risk specific to one business or sector, reducible by diversifying a portfolio
Risk affecting the entire market, which can't be fully eliminated just by diversifying stocks
Allocating capital across many different assets/sectors to reduce a portfolio's overall risk
How much two assets move together or oppositely; low correlation makes diversification more effective

lines: Diversification doesn't eliminate risk entirely, but it eliminates the unnecessary risk - the risk specific to each business that you aren't compensated extra to bear.
A multi-sector portfolio or a broad-index ETF is always a safer starting point than dumping all your capital into one stock, no matter how attractive that stock seems.
